docs.title: Airport Management System
docs.text:
Author(s):

(TODO) Your Name <your-email -at- thapar -dot- edu>

A multi-module airport operations platform — Ops Core, Booking, Baggage, Connecting Flights, Emergency Handling, Accessibility, Staff & Employee Management, Parking, Facilities, Security, a Support Chatbot, Predictive Analytics, and an Admin Dashboard — all built on one shared operational data layer (Airport, Gate, Flight, Passenger, Resource, User). See Week 1 scope for the full module list and tiering, and ERD for the schema diagram.

docs.text: Layer Choice Backend Node.js + Express Database PostgreSQL Real-time Socket.IO (WebSockets) Frontend React (Vite) Auth JWT, roles: passenger, ground_crew, security, medical, ops_manager, admin Testing Jest (backend), React Testing Library (frontend) Deployment Backend → Render/Railway, Frontend → Vercel, DB → managed Postgres

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Open the frontend URL — you should see the API status card with db.connected: true. Register a passenger account, then promote it to admin directly in the database (see code/backend/src/routes/auth.js for why there's no public admin-creation route) to explore the Staff Management, shift scheduling, and attendance panels.

docs.title: Progress so far
docs.text:
• Week 1 — scope finalized across 15 modules (tiered by engineering depth), full ERD, complete Postgres schema, backend/frontend skeleton with a live /health check.
  • Week 2 — JWT auth (register/login/me), Staff & Employee Management (records, shift scheduling with overlap-conflict rejection, unit tested), Attendance clock-in/clock-out, and role-aware frontend (login/register pages, dashboard with passenger/staff/admin views).

See the journals for the week-by-week engineering log.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Notes for the report
docs.text:
• User is the auth/identity table (JWT, roles). Employee and Passenger are role-specific profile extensions of User — this avoids duplicating auth logic per role, which is worth a sentence in the architecture section of the report.
  • Flight is the busiest table in the schema by relationship count — it's touched by Ops Core, Booking, Delay, Connections, Emergency, and Predictive Analytics. That fan-out is exactly the "one shared core, many views" claim from the architecture doc, and it's visible directly in the diagram, which makes it an easy thing to point to when a grader asks how the modules integrate.

docs.title: Airport Management System — Week 1: Scope & Setup
1. Project scope
docs.text:
Twelve modules, sharing one operational core (Airport, Gate, Flight, Passenger, Resource, User). No module owns a silo of data — they all read/write the shared core, which is the architectural point being demonstrated.

# Module Tier Owner-side users 1 Ops Core (flights, gates, resources, turnaround) 1 Admin / Ops 2 Booking Portal (search, seat lock, mock pay, e-ticket) 1 Passengers 3 Delay handling + cascading recalculation 1 Ops 4 Connecting Flights (min connection time, at-risk/missed) 1 Passengers / Ops 5 Emergency Handling (declare/alert/resolve) 1 Ops / Security / Admin 6 Predictive Analytics (delay + congestion forecasting) 1 Ops manager 7 Support Chatbot (live data lookup + escalation) 1 Passengers 8 Baggage Management (tag + status pipeline) 2 Ground staff / Passengers 9 Check-in (web check-in, boarding pass, no-show) 2 Passengers 10 Accessibility & Medical Assistance (request queue) 2 Passengers / Ground staff 11 Staff & Employee Management (shifts, attendance) 2 Admin / HR 12 Parking Management (slots, concurrency-safe booking) 2 Passengers / Admin 13 Facilities Directory (lounges, shops, restrooms) 2 Passengers 14 Security Module (checkpoints, screening, incidents) 2 Security staff 15 Admin Dashboard (rolls up everything above) — Ops manager

Tier 1 gets the engineering depth (concurrency, cascading logic, real-time updates, prediction). Tier 2 is CRUD + status pipelines done correctly but simply. This split is intentional and is called out explicitly so it reads as a planned decision, not a shortcut taken under deadline pressure.

docs.title: Week 1 : Scope, ERD, Schema & Skeleton Deploy
Goal
docs.text: Finalize the project scope, design the shared data model, and stand up a deployable backend/frontend skeleton before any feature work begins.

docs.title: What was done
docs.text:
• Locked the scope to 15 modules (Ops Core, Booking, Baggage, Connecting Flights, Emergency Handling, Predictive Analytics, Support Chatbot, Check-in, Accessibility & Medical Assistance, Staff & Employee Management, Parking, Facilities Directory, Security, Admin Dashboard), split into Tier 1 (engineering depth — concurrency, cascading logic, real-time updates, prediction) and Tier 2 (CRUD + status pipelines). See docs/week1-scope.md.
  • Chose the shared operational core: Airport, Gate, Flight, Passenger, Resource, User — every module reads/writes this core instead of owning a private data silo.
  • Locked the tech stack: Node.js + Express, PostgreSQL, Socket.IO, React (Vite), JWT auth with six roles, Jest / React Testing Library for tests.
  • Wrote the full ERD covering all 15 modules' entities (docs/erd.md) and the corresponding CREATE TABLE migration (code/db/schema.sql).
  • Scaffolded the repo: code/backend (Express) and code/frontend (React/Vite), with a skeleton /health endpoint on the backend and a skeleton frontend page that calls it and renders db.connected.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: The Tier 1 / Tier 2 split was made explicit up front rather than discovered under deadline pressure later — Tier 1 modules are where the harder engineering problems (conflict detection, cascading recalculation, real-time state) are demonstrated; Tier 2 modules prove the same data layer supports simpler CRUD flows cleanly.

docs.title: Outstanding / carried to Week 2
docs.text:
• Live deployment (backend → Render/Railway, frontend → Vercel, DB → managed Postgres) — instructions are documented in the root README.md, to be executed from the team's own hosting accounts.
  • Auth (JWT, six roles) and the first real feature module — Staff & Employee Management.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Add JWT authentication and the first real feature module — Staff & Employee Management, including shift scheduling and attendance.

docs.title: What was done
docs.text:
Backend

  • POST /auth/register (public, passenger accounts only), POST /auth/login, GET /auth/me.
  • src/middleware/auth.js — authenticate, requireAuth, requireRole(...) — shared by every protected route from here on.
  • POST /employees (admin) — creates a User (staff role) + Employee record together and returns a one-time temp password; GET /employees, GET /employees/:id (admin, ops_manager); PATCH /employees/:id/status (admin).
  • POST /shifts (admin, ops_manager) — rejects overlapping shifts for the same employee with 409 plus the conflicting rows; GET /shifts, GET /shifts/mine, DELETE /shifts/:id.
  • POST /attendance/clock-in, POST /attendance/clock-out, GET /attendance.
  • src/services/shiftConflict.js — the overlap-check logic, unit tested in tests/shiftConflict.test.js. This is the same pattern planned for resource_assignment (Week 3) and parking-slot booking (Week 7).

Frontend

  • AuthContext — token kept in localStorage, validated against /auth/me on load.
  • /login, /register pages.
  • /dashboard, role-aware: passengers see a welcome card; staff see "My shifts" with clock in/out; admin/ops_manager see the shift scheduler; admin additionally sees staff management (create account
  • roster).

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: There is deliberately no public route to create an admin account (see code/backend/src/routes/auth.js) — the first admin has to be bootstrapped directly in the database after registering a normal passenger account, which keeps privilege escalation out of the public API surface entirely.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: shiftConflict.js's overlap-detection logic is covered by unit tests (code/backend/tests/shiftConflict.test.js), runnable with npm test — no database needed, since the conflict check is pure logic over time ranges.

docs.title: Outstanding / carried forward
docs.text:
• Resource assignment and parking-slot booking will reuse the same conflict-check pattern established here (Weeks 3 and 7).
  • Remaining Tier 1 modules (Booking, Delay handling, Connecting Flights, Emergency Handling, Predictive Analytics, Chatbot) not yet started.

docs.title: Week 3 : Ops Core — Flights, Gates, Turnaround & Resources
Goal
docs.text: Build the core scheduling engine: flights, gates, gate auto-assignment with size-compatibility and conflict checking, the turnaround checklist, and resource (fuel truck / baggage cart / crew) allocation with the same no-double-booking rule as Week 2's shifts.

docs.title: What was done
docs.text:
Backend

  • airport, aircraft_type: reference data, admin-managed (GET/POST /airports, GET/POST /aircraft-types).
  • GET/POST /gates, PATCH /gates/:id/status (admin, ops_manager).
  • src/services/sizeCompat.js — gateCanHost(aircraftSize, gateSize) (a gate can host an aircraft at or below its own size class) and TURNAROUND_MINUTES per size class, used by both gate-window calculation and the turnaround checklist's estimated durations.
  • src/services/gateConflict.js — computeGateWindow() (buffer around scheduled departure, sized by aircraft class) and checkGateConflict(), reusing rangesOverlap from Week 2's shiftConflict.js rather than redefining it.
  • src/services/gateAssignment.js — suggestGate(): greedy smallest-compatible-first search over a gate list, using checkGateConflict to skip busy gates.
  • POST /flights — auto-assigns a gate when gate_id is omitted; when supplied, validates it through the same compatibility + conflict checks as the auto path, so a manual request can't bypass the rule. Also auto-generates the turnaround checklist (src/services/turnaround.js) on creation.
  • GET /flights, GET /flights/:id (with checklist), PATCH /flights/:id/gate (reassignment, re-validated), PATCH /flights/:id/status.
  • PATCH /turnaround/:id/status — ground_crew can now write, not just read; marking a step done accepts an explicit actual_duration_minutes (see "Known simplification" below).
  • src/services/resourceConflict.js — same overlap pattern as shiftConflict.js, applied to resource_assignment.
  • POST /resources, GET /resources, PATCH /resources/:id/status; POST/GET/DELETE /resource-assignments with conflict checking.
  • scripts/seed.js — 3 airports, 3 aircraft types, 6 gates (mixed sizes) so the demo has something to actually conflict over.

Frontend

  • pages/OpsCore.jsx (admin, ops_manager): reference-data quick-add, gate manager, flight scheduler (auto-assign toggle, conflict errors surfaced with the specific conflicting flight), resource manager.
  • pages/OpsCore.jsx also exports TurnaroundBoard (ground_crew): a simple pending-tasks list with a "mark done" action.
  • Wired into Dashboard.jsx alongside the Week 2 sections.

docs.title: Key decision
docs.text: The gate-conflict rule is enforced identically whether a gate is auto-assigned or manually typed in by an ops manager — the manual path calls the exact same checkGateConflict / gateCanHost functions the auto-suggest path uses. This was a deliberate choice: a conflict rule that only applies to one entry path isn't a real rule.

docs.title: Known simplification
docs.text: This schema stores one gate per flight leg (assigned around departure), not separate arrival/departure gate legs — a flight's "ground window" is modeled as a buffer before/after scheduled_departure, sized by aircraft class, rather than tracking true gate occupancy from touchdown to pushback. Documented in gateConflict.js. Also, turnaround_checklist has no started_at column yet, so actual_duration is supplied by the caller when marking a step done rather than computed from elapsed time — adding those timestamp columns is a named follow-up for Week 5, when delay cascading needs "did a step run over its estimate" as a signal.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
sizeCompat.test.js (pure), gateConflict.test.js, gateAssignment.test.js, resourceConflict.test.js — all mock-DB-backed like Week 2's shiftConflict.test.js. 30 tests total across the suite (Week 2 + Week 3), all passing.

Beyond unit tests, the full flow was verified against a real local Postgres instance (schema → seed → live API calls): auto-assign correctly skips a busy or size-incompatible gate and lands on the next compatible one; a manual gate request on an occupied gate is rejected with 409 and the specific conflicting flight; a resource double-booking is rejected the same way; turnaround steps update correctly. Screenshots/transcript in the Week 3 report.

docs.title: Outstanding / carried forward
docs.text:
• Resource assignment doesn't yet check aircraft/turnaround-step compatibility (e.g. a crew resource assigned to a fuel step) — it only prevents double-booking the resource itself. Fine for now; worth a line in the final report as a scoping decision.
  • Remaining Tier 1 modules (Booking, Delay cascading, Connecting Flights, Emergency Handling, Predictive Analytics, Chatbot) not yet started — next up is Week 4 (Booking + Check-in).

docs.title: Progress Report — Step 0: Fix Existing Problems & System Hardening
docs.text: Branch: step0 Date: 2026-11-12 Status: Completed & Verified (All tests passing, builds clean, live PostgreSQL verified)

docs.title: 1. What Was Built (Mapped to Plan & Step 0 Requirements)
docs.text:
• 1. Advisory Transaction Locks for Concurrency Safety:
  • Implemented pg_advisory_xact_lock(domain, id) within single transaction clients for:
    • Shifts (routes/shifts.js using ADVISORY_LOCK_DOMAINS.EMPLOYEE)
    • Resource assignments (routes/resourceAssignments.js using ADVISORY_LOCK_DOMAINS.RESOURCE)
    • Gate assignments & reassignments (routes/flights.js using ADVISORY_LOCK_DOMAINS.GATE)
  • Updated conflict detection services (shiftConflict.js, resourceConflict.js, gateConflict.js, gateAssignment.js) to execute against the same transactional client.
  • 2. Unified Real Fares & Snapshots:
  • Added flight.base_price_cents (default 5000) and booking.price_cents to schema.
  • Implemented class multipliers: Economy (\(1.0\times\)), Premium Economy (\(1.4\times\)), Business (\(2.2\times\)), First (\(3.5\times\)).
  • Search (/bookings/search-flights), seat map (/bookings/flights/:flightId/seats), booking execution, and payment record now use identical deterministic pricing and snapshot the charged amount at booking creation.
  • 3. Route Input Validation:
  • Added Zod schemas with unified middleware (middleware/validate.js) ensuring flight_id and seat_id are validated positive integers.
  • Returns standard HTTP 400 with { error: 'Validation failed', details: [...] }.
  • 4. Seat Generation Race Safety & Aircraft Type Capacity:
  • Created services/seatService.js to automatically pre-generate all seats inside the flight creation transaction (POST /flights).
  • Seat layouts and capacities match the actual aircraft types (ATR 72: 78 seats; Airbus A320: 180 seats; Boeing 777: 396 seats).
  • Added database migration 002_step0_hardening.sql backfilling seats for existing flights.
  • 5. Flight Status State Machine & Cancellation Cascades:
  • Enforced strict state transitions (scheduled \(\to\) boarding / delayed / cancelled, etc.) in PATCH /flights/:id/status.
  • When a flight transitions to cancelled, an atomic cascade executes:
    • Gate is released (gate_id = NULL).
    • Resource assignments are deleted.
    • Active bookings are updated to 'cancelled'.
    • Successful payments are marked 'refunded'.
    • Booked seats are freed (is_booked = false).
    • WebSocket events flight:status_updated and flight:cancelled are emitted.
  • 6. Emergency Resolution Permissions & Employee Attribution:
  • Restricted PATCH /emergencies/:id/resolve to alerted roles, admin, or ops_manager. Non-alerted roles attempting resolution receive HTTP 403 Forbidden.
  • Updated emergency_alert with acknowledged_by INTEGER REFERENCES "user"(id).
  • PATCH /emergencies/:id/acknowledge records both acknowledged_at and acknowledged_by.
  • 7. Assistance Status Staff Assignment Fix:
  • Updated PATCH /bookings/assistance/:id/status so assigned_staff_id is assigned when transitioning to 'assigned', and preserved without overwrite on subsequent transitions (in_progress, completed).
  • 8. Cryptographic Booking References:
  • Replaced Math.random() with crypto.randomBytes(6) generating unambiguous base32 Crockford-style references (BK + 6 chars).
  • Added unique constraint retry loop.
  • 9. Passenger Table Linkage (Option B):
  • Added booking.passenger_id REFERENCES passenger(id).
  • Added Stitch registry columns (passport_number, nationality, date_of_birth, created_at) to passenger.
  • Backfilled existing bookings with passenger records.
  • 10. Security Hardening & Pagination:
  • Installed and configured helmet for security headers.
  • Added rate limiting: 1000 req/15min globally, 30 req/15min on /auth/login and /auth/register.
  • Enforced production security check: server refuses to start if NODE_ENV === 'production' and JWT_SECRET is missing or default.
  • Added pagination (limit default 50, offset default 0) to all list endpoints.
  • Restricted CORS and Socket.IO origin to FRONTEND_URL.
  • 11. Numbered Database Migration System:
  • Created code/backend/migrations/:
    • 001_initial_schema.sql (safe baseline with IF NOT EXISTS)
    • 002_step0_hardening.sql (fares, seat backfill, passenger linkage, alert attribution)
  • Created code/backend/scripts/migrate.js tracking executed migrations in schema_migrations.
  • Added "migrate": "node scripts/migrate.js" to package.json.
  • 12. Constants & Refactoring:
  • Created code/backend/src/constants/index.js consolidating roles, lock domains, and status transitions.
  • Extracted code/backend/src/services/bookingService.js.
  • Updated API root message to show current version (0.2.0) and operational modules.
  • Cross-platform test runner: updated "test" script to use ./node_modules/jest/bin/jest.js --runInBand --forceExit.

docs.title: Week 6 — Connecting Flights & IRROPS Rebooking
docs.text: Branch: week6-connections Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: What Was Built (mapped to plan)
docs.text: Plan Item Implementation Airport Minimum Connection Time (MCT) Migration 005_week5_delays_and_connections.sql and 006_week6_airport_mcts.sql added min_connection_minutes to airport table with realistic per-airport standards: BOM = 45m, DEL = 60m, BLR = 40m (no invented terminals). Connecting Itinerary Validation validateAndCreateConnection() in connectionService.js strictly validates geometry: inbound.dest_id === outbound.origin_id (rejecting mismatches with clear HTTP 400). Computes initial layover time vs airport MCT and assigns initial status (on_track, at_risk, or missed). Status Rules & Cascade Integration Status logic: missed if actual layover < 20 min (gate closing) or either flight cancelled; at_risk if actual layover < airport MCT; on_track otherwise. reEvaluateConnectionsForFlight() is invoked automatically from delayCascadeService.js whenever inbound flights are delayed, dynamically advancing estimated arrival times and emitting connection:status_changed real-time events. Rebooking Suggestions Engine getRebookingOptions() dynamically scans alternative flights from transit hub to destination: scheduled after inbound.estimated_arrival + hub.mct, excluding cancelled/departed flights, requiring available inventory, and sorting by passenger cabin class match and earliest departure (up to 3 real slots). Atomic Transactional Rebooking rebookConnection() runs inside a single database transaction: acquires PostgreSQL advisory lock pg_advisory_xact_lock(5, newSeatId) to prevent double-booking races, row-locks connection with FOR UPDATE OF c, verifies seat availability, cancels old outbound booking, frees old seat, creates new confirmed booking, writes a $0 payment row with status = 'success' for zero-fee IRROPS protection, updates connection, and broadcasts live socket event. Admin Connections Endpoint GET /connections/admin/at-risk restricted to admin and ops_manager: returns real aggregate metrics (monitored, at_risk, missed, rebooked_today) and filtered connections with search and hub filtering. Rebook Missed Connection Modal RebookConnectionModal.jsx matching Stitch layout: displays original outbound booking to be cancelled, up to 3 real alternative flights with radio selection, ₹0 protection indicator, explicit confirmation button, and robust handling for "no options available" and "seat locking conflict / try again". No one-click or simulated rebooking. My Flights Connecting Itinerary View MyFlights.jsx renders multi-segment connecting itineraries in authentic perforated ticket-notch card format with inbound segment, layover connector node (actual layover vs airport MCT, shortfall/deficit badge), outbound segment, and status banners (at_risk in amber, missed in red, on_track in emerald). Admin Connections at Risk Dashboard AdminConnections.jsx matching Stitch layout: real KPI metric cards, status segmented tabs, hub pills (All Hubs, BOM, DEL, BLR), passenger search, and real data table with zero hardcoded values. Rebook buttons omitted awaiting user architecture approval. Real-time Navigation & Sockets Added "Connections at Risk" link to Admin sidebar (AdminLayout.jsx) and registered /admin/connections route (App.jsx). Real-time socket subscriptions update views instantly when delay cascades occur.

docs.title: Deliberately Omitted from Stitch Designs (and Rationale)
docs.text:
Per user instructions and project principles (production quality, zero fake/hardcoded data), the following elements were intentionally excluded:

  1. Demo Controls & Switchers: - Removed: "Sim State Switcher", "Screen States Tester", "Simulation View" toggle, "Restore Demo", and fake sync timers. - Rationale: All application states (loading, empty, on track, at risk, missed, conflict/error) are driven by real API responses and database queries.

  2. Invented Services & Ancillary Add-ons: - Removed: Electric buggy / "Ping Cart", BOM Concierge, Transfer Desk locator, transit hotel and meal vouchers, lounge access, dining credit, Gate Runner Dispatch, SMS/WhatsApp boarding pass sending. - Rationale: None of these services exist in the project scope or database schema.

  3. Data Not Supported by Schema: - Removed: Terminals (T1, T2, T3), gate walking times, terminal transfer map, flight distance km, aircraft amenities (Wi-Fi, USB power), meal preference dropdowns, seat position tags ("Window"), boarding close time. - Rationale: Schema models gates and airports directly without terminal divisions. All display data strictly comes from existing database columns.

  4. Deferred Features & Upgrade Schemes: - Removed: Checked baggage tracking cards, tags, and progress bars (deferred to Week 7 baggage milestone). - Removed: Business-class upgrade with extra fee (+₹1,200), pre-reserved standby seats, complete PDF itinerary download, "Instant Reschedule (₹0)" one-click action. - Rationale: IRROPS rebooking is passenger-confirmed with explicit radio selection; baggage tracking is scheduled for Week 7.

  5. Fake Telemetry & Marketing Claims: - Removed: "Live Telemetry Feed (VOMM ATC)", "Concourse Transit Index", "Avg auto-reroute latency", "Meridian Seamless Connect Guarantee", "Transit Protocol §4.2", "Zero Penalty Protection", and hardcoded dummy passenger names/counts (e.g. 142 monitored transfers, Rajesh Sharma). - Rationale: All metric counters and table rows reflect live PostgreSQL data.

  6. Terminal-Based MCT Legend: - Removed: "MCT Criteria: BOM Domestic-to-Domestic = 45m · DEL T3 Inter-Terminal = 60m". - Rationale: Standardized to airport-level min_connection_minutes (BOM 45, DEL 60, BLR 40).

  7. Staff Rebooking Buttons on Admin Table: - Removed: "Rebook Passenger" and "Priority Rebook" buttons from the admin table. - Rationale: Kept read-only pending user architectural decision regarding staff permissions, audit logging, and passenger notification.

docs.title: Manual Verification Steps
docs.text:
1. Database Seed: Run npm run seed in code/backend to seed airports (BOM 45m, DEL 60m, BLR 40m), flights, and an at-risk connecting itinerary for Passenger 1 (AI-101 DEL \(\rightarrow\) BOM delayed by 38m, connecting to 6E-202 BOM \(\rightarrow\) BLR with 32m actual layover vs 45m BOM MCT).
  2. Passenger Portal (/my-flights): - Log in as passenger@example.com. - Observe amber "Connection At Risk" banner with 32m actual vs 45m MCT and -13m deficit. - Click "View Rebooking Options" to open modal. - Select alternative flight AI-504 and click "Confirm Rebooking (Flight AI-504)". - Observe atomic cancellation of 6E-202, seat reassignment to AI-504, ₹0 payment snapshot, and connection status flipping to on_track.
  3. Admin Dashboard (/admin/connections): - Log in as admin (admin@example.com). - Navigate to "Connections at Risk" in the sidebar menu. - Verify KPI cards (monitored, at_risk, missed, rebooked_today) match database counts. - Test filters (All Alerts, At Risk, Missed, BOM hub, passenger search).
